units.title: Understand the people and the place
units.output: An agreed brief, evidence notes and an existing-features map.
units.context: Status: three new English reserve lessons. Not published, translated, narrated or learner-tested. Sources and exclusions are in SOURCES.md. Read CASEBOOK.md before using the worked examples.

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: A drawing contains a pond, orchard, poultry area and many beds. The household asked for food near home and less carrying. Has the drawing answered the brief?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
A brief says what the design should help people do. Begin by listening. Ask who uses the place, what is already working and what is difficult. Ask about food, movement, care work and what people want to protect. People may value privacy, a familiar gathering place or a clear route as much as another growing area.

Include the people who do the work. Do not ask only the person who speaks first. A proposal that relies on another person's daily labour needs their agreement. Ask what happens when the usual carer is away. Keep private household information out of a public course example.

Separate a need from an idea. “We need a reliable way to water the existing garden” states a need. “We need a new tank” suggests one possible response. The response still needs information about supply, demand, location, cost and care. Drawing it does not answer those questions.

Write the priorities in plain language, or record them with consent as an oral explanation. Say what is outside this first phase. Record available resources as known, reported or still unknown. Read the brief back to the household and invite corrections. Disagreement is useful information; do not hide it to finish the sheet.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: BRIEF-A in the busy-yard case prioritises food, clear access and manageable care. The household has not asked for animals. RESOURCES-A has no budget or care-time figures. The learner writes “confirm care time and costs”, not an invented amount, and keeps the route in the brief.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Make a brief with spaces for people and uses, priorities, things to protect, agreed scope, available resources, and questions still open. Use the practice case or obtain consent for a real household exercise. A partner reads it back. Change anything that misrepresents the household.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Does agreement on the brief establish permission to alter a neighbour's drainage route? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** the brief records household aims; permissions and effects beyond the site need their own checks.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner distinguishes needs from proposed objects, includes the people doing the work, and leaves missing resources visible. A list of attractive features alone does not pass this task.

sections.title: App companion
sections.text: Getting started and evidence guides. A paper brief is valid; do not put private household details into a public sample.

lessons.title: Observe, ask and keep the source

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: A resident describes water crossing the yard during heavy rain. The visit is dry. How should that information appear in the notes?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
Observation starts with what is there. Walk safely with someone who knows the place. Look at routes, water points, ground cover, shade, buildings, growing areas and signs of past use. Listen to the people who use the site. A short visit and a long memory offer different evidence.

Keep those differences visible. “I saw this” is an observation. “The resident described this” is a report. “I measured this” needs the method and unit. “I think this may happen” is an interpretation. “I want to put this here” is a proposal. All can be useful, but they are not interchangeable.

Record when and under what conditions you observed. A shaded patch during one visit is not a full seasonal sunlight record. A dry water point on one day does not by itself explain the cause or the whole year's supply. Look again when it is safe and useful. Do not wait for perfect knowledge before keeping a record, and do not pretend a short visit supplies it.

Use a notebook, labelled drawing or consented photograph. Give each piece of evidence a short reference you can put on the map. If a plant, pipe or boundary is uncertain, label the uncertainty. Do not identify a plant or underground service from an attractive illustration.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: WALK-A records the route and carried containers as seen. TALK-A records the resident's rain account as reported. The learner does not turn that account into a measured contour or flood depth. Further investigation becomes an action in the evidence register.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: For each note, record the feature, what is known, how it is known, source/conditions, and what needs checking. Ask a partner to point out any sentence where a guess sounds like a measured fact. Correct the label, not the evidence.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Is “water always comes from this direction” justified by one dry-day visit? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** the statement exceeds the evidence. Record the account and seek appropriate observations or assessment.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner distinguishes observed, reported, measured, inferred and proposed information, and names a useful next check. More photographs do not automatically mean better evidence.

sections.title: App companion
sections.text: Evidence guide. Preserve the source with the feature; exporting a picture does not verify the information in it.

lessons.title: Make a base map you can trust

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: A learner moves an existing path on a base map to make room for a proposed bed. What information has been lost?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
A base map shows the place before the proposed changes. It helps everyone discuss the same site. Show the existing buildings, access routes, water points, growing areas and other features that matter to the brief. Mark north when you have checked it, and keep the source of the boundary visible.

A first sketch may help you understand relationships. Label it “not to scale” if that is what it is. Before using a plan to judge fit, check the measurements and use a consistent scale. Keep units with dimensions. Measure relevant widths and distances safely, and record whether a value was measured, taken from a source or estimated. A precise-looking line is not proof of a precise measurement.

Keep the existing map and the proposal separate. A transparent sheet over paper, a saved copy or a clearly labelled proposal layer lets you try ideas while preserving what is actually there. Do not silently shift the house, path or boundary to make an idea fit. A traced satellite picture can be a starting reference; it does not by itself establish legal ownership or a surveyed boundary.

Give the map a title, date or revision, legend and source notes. Use words as well as colour so a printed or colour-blind reader can distinguish existing features, proposed changes and uncertain information. Leave enough space for labels to be read.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: MAP-A is useful for discussion but lacks dimensions and verified orientation. The learner keeps its “not to scale” label and lists the measurements needed. They cannot claim a new bed fits simply because a small rectangle fits on the sketch.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Make the existing-features map and a separate blank proposal sheet. Match each important feature to a note from D1.2. If measurement is unavailable, identify the missing measurement and the decision it prevents. For a real site, retain the original measurements when trying a new layout.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Can a neat exported map turn an estimated boundary into a surveyed one? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** export changes presentation, not the source or certainty of the boundary.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: Existing and proposed features remain distinct; scale status, orientation status, units and source notes are explicit. Fit is not asserted without the relevant measurements.

sections.title: App companion
sections.text: Mapping and design guides. Practise on a copy or sample first. Verify the saved feature and its measurements after editing; use Undo for an accidental edit rather than accepting a convenient distortion.

units.title: Read patterns and constraints
units.output: Analysis overlays and design questions with their missing checks.
units.context: Status: three new English reserve lessons. D1 supplies the brief, evidence register and base map. These lessons analyse that evidence; they do not provide engineering, fire-management or water-permission instructions.

lessons.title: Use zones and sectors for different questions

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: One arrow follows a daily watering journey. Another marks a reported wind direction. Do they describe the same kind of information?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
Zone planning considers how people use and care for things. Something needing frequent attention should be considered in relation to the routes people already take. Look at the actual work: visiting, watering, harvesting, feeding, carrying and checking. A short distance on paper may still be awkward if there is a steep step, a locked gate or an obstructed path.

Zones are a thinking tool, not compulsory rings. A small site does not need to contain every zone. Do not assign a fixed zone to every animal or crop without considering its care and the household. The placement must also suit the element's other needs.

Sector analysis considers influences such as sun, wind, incoming water and neighbouring activities. Use the evidence for this site. Label a direction as observed, reported or still needing confirmation. A regional description is not proof that the wind at this particular home always comes from one direction.

Put the layers beside each other. Convenience may suggest a place near the home; shade, access or other constraints may make that place unsuitable. This is a question to resolve, not a reason to ignore one of the layers. Explain both the benefit and the limitation of a proposed position.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: WALK-A shows containers carried to the existing patch. That supports investigating the care journey. The eastern shade snapshot and TALK-A's water report remain separate evidence. Neither gives enough information to declare a new growing position suitable.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: On one overlay, draw actual care journeys and note their purpose and frequency from the household record. On another, show the relevant external influences and evidence sources. Name a place where two needs may conflict. Keep uncertain information visibly uncertain.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Must a small homestead contain all the zones to be a valid design? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** the tool helps organise real activities and care; the site and household determine what belongs there.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner explains the difference between a care journey and an external influence, uses site evidence, and identifies a placement trade-off.

sections.title: App companion
sections.text: Design guide, Base and Sector stages. Adding an arrow is a way to record a claim, not a way to verify it.

lessons.title: Read water, access and seasons together

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: The most convenient route to a proposed garden crosses a place where water is reported during heavy rain. What needs checking before choosing that layout?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
A design brings different observations together. Trace how people reach the places they use, where water is observed or reported, and where shade changes. Consider how the same arrangement might work in different conditions. Keep a useful access route in view while thinking about a new growing area.

The position of a water point does not tell you how much suitable water is reliably available. A tank drawn higher on a map is not necessarily higher on the ground. A flow arrow does not supply levels, soil information, a safe outlet or permission to redirect water. Those questions need appropriate evidence and, where relevant, qualified help. Keep drainage and construction proposals separate from what is already known.

A photograph of a green site does not prove year-round supply. Ask what changes during dry periods, rain, cold or household absence. Use local records and the existing seasonal-planning lessons to decide what else to observe. Do not copy a calendar or a fixed compass rule from another place without checking its relevance.

Some constraints change the scope of a proposal. If water, access or care is unresolved, improving a smaller existing area may be worth comparing with expansion. Deferring a feature can be a sound design decision. Explain the missing evidence and the next action so “later” does not mean forgotten.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The busy-yard learner keeps the used route clear on every concept. They mark the eastern water report for further investigation rather than drawing a trench. They ask about the reliability and suitability of the existing supply before promising a larger garden.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Choose one proposed use. Trace the person's journey, the water it would need and the evidence about its location. List what is known, what could change seasonally, and what must be checked before implementation. Refer to the water, soil and seasonal modules for the technical questions.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Does drawing a swale settle whether it is suitable or safe to build? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** a drawing cannot replace terrain, soil, water, outlet and permission checks or relevant qualified assessment.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner connects access, care and environmental information without inventing a design threshold or treating an unresolved technical proposal as ready to build.

sections.title: App companion
sections.text: Mapping, design and crop-planning guides. Keep a proposed water feature labelled as proposed; do not mistake software availability for site suitability.

lessons.title: Turn observations into decisions worth testing

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: “Put a new bed here” gives a location. “How can we grow food without blocking access or adding more care than we can manage?” gives a design question. Which helps compare options?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
Analysis turns the brief and evidence into questions that can guide a design. For each important observation, explain why it matters to the household. Then identify a possible response and what would need to be true for that response to work.

Keep the chain visible: need, evidence, implication, possible response, missing check. If a step is missing, return to it. A learner may notice that a route is used frequently, but still need to ask who uses it and what they carry before changing its shape.

Use the ethics in a practical way. Who gains from a proposal? Who takes on more work? What existing life, soil, water or shared resource could be harmed? A benefit for one element may create a problem elsewhere. Do not call a system sustainable simply because it has many features or recycles something.

Write criteria before choosing your favourite drawing. Criteria come from the brief and site evidence: access remains usable, care is agreed, water needs can be met, and important unknowns are resolved or the affected work is deferred. A criterion needs evidence. “Looks natural” alone does not demonstrate that the household can maintain it.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The question becomes: “Can the existing patch work better while keeping the route usable?” The learner also keeps relocation and deferring expansion available for comparison. BRIEF-A supports manageable care; WALK-A supports the access concern; RESOURCES-A prevents a claim that expansion is affordable. None of these facts yet chooses the final layout.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Make a decision sheet with columns for the need, evidence reference, implication, possible responses and missing checks. Ask a partner to challenge a response: “What evidence would make you change your mind?” Keep the answer for the concept comparison in D3.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Is choosing the design with the most components a fair test of quality? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** the components must answer the brief and work together within the site's and household's limits.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner traces a decision back to evidence, names a trade-off and a reason to revise. The facilitator asks for a fresh explanation if the learner only repeats a principle's name.

sections.title: App companion
sections.text: Evidence and design guides. The decision sheet can stay on paper with an exported map. It is the explanation of the plan, not an automatic result produced by the app.

units.title: Connect functions and compare options
units.output: Connections, alternative concepts and a reasoned choice.
units.context: Status: three English reserve drafts. D1–D2 supply the household brief, base map and analysis. The worked case is illustrative; final measured layouts and visual demonstrations remain to be produced.

lessons.title: Ask what each part needs and gives

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: Compost is placed beside a garden on a drawing. What would make that relationship useful in daily work?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
A useful connection is more than a line between two objects. Ask what each part needs, what it produces, who cares for it and how things move between the parts. A compost area may receive suitable material and supply finished compost, but someone must sort, carry and manage it. Its position must allow that work and suit local hygiene and site conditions.

Write needs and outputs beside the elements you are considering. Include water, suitable materials, space, access, time and skills. Do not count an output before it is available and suitable for its intended use. A proposed animal system does not provide free fertility: animals also require care, feed, water, welfare and management of wastes.

Look for useful connections, but also conflicts. A convenient position might obstruct a route. One person's useful output might create another person's handling burden. A connection that needs daily attention can fail if nobody agrees to provide it. Keep bought inputs and materials leaving the site in the picture; a neat cycle diagram does not prove that everything is supplied on site.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The busy yard already connects the home, water point and growing patch through a carrying route. Before adding another system, the learner asks whether the current care journey can be improved. BRIEF-A excludes animals from this phase, so livestock are not added to complete a decorative cycle.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Draw the needs, outputs, journeys and responsible people for the elements in your brief. Circle an assumed connection and name the evidence needed to confirm it. Use the appropriate technical module before proposing a material's use.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Does an arrow from animals to a garden prove that the garden needs no other fertility inputs? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** amounts, suitability, losses, other inputs and crop requirements have not been established.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner explains a real connection, its care requirement and a possible conflict, without promising a closed or maintenance-free system.

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: A learner has drawn one beautiful arrangement. What can they compare it with to decide whether it answers the brief well?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
A first idea is a starting point. Make different concept arrangements while changes are still easy. Keep the same brief, base map and evidence for each. A comparison is unfair if one option receives an imaginary water supply or unpaid labour while the other must use the recorded resources.

A concept shows the main relationships and intended uses. It does not yet settle every dimension or technical detail. Use a proposal overlay so existing features remain visible. Label what is retained, changed, added or deferred. Keep unresolved matters beside the affected part of each option.

Make the alternatives genuinely useful. They might compare improving an existing growing area with relocating it, or a modest first phase with later expansion. Do not make one option deliberately foolish so your favourite wins. Keeping the present arrangement while gathering evidence can also be a reasonable option.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: Busy-yard concept A improves care of the existing patch while preserving access. Concept B investigates a different location, also preserving access. B must still answer the water report, shade, soil, measurement and care questions; A must still answer whether the existing patch can meet the household's priorities. Neither receives a promised harvest or invented cost advantage.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Draw alternative concepts on copies of the same base. Under each, write its intended benefit, likely burden, important unknown and what would rule it out. Ask a partner whether both options use the same evidence.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Can a concept be called cheaper when its material quantities and costs are missing? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** “cost unknown” must stay visible until a comparable estimate is supported.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: Alternatives differ meaningfully, preserve existing facts and are compared on equal assumptions. Sketches remain labelled as concepts rather than build-ready plans.

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: One option looks better in a rendered picture. The other better preserves daily access. What should the decision record explain?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
Compare the options against the criteria you wrote from the brief. Start with needs that cannot be traded away: usable access, agreed care, required permissions and a proposal's basic suitability. Then consider benefits, burdens, costs and what may change over time.

Use words and evidence references. “Possible, but water evidence is missing” is more honest than a precise-looking score with no basis. If you use a scoring exercise, agree what each score means and who chooses the priorities. Adding scores must not cancel an unresolved safety or permission requirement.

Ask the household to explain the choice in its own words. A designer's preference should not quietly replace the household's priorities. Record why an option was chosen, why another was set aside and what new information could change the decision. A conditional choice is valid when its condition is clear and the affected work waits.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The busy-yard household provisionally prefers investigating improvements to the existing patch because the brief values manageable care and keeping access. This is not proof of lower cost or higher yield. Relocation remains available if later measurements or site assessment show the existing patch cannot meet the brief.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Complete a comparison sheet: criterion, supporting evidence, implication for each option, remaining check and decision. Present the strongest argument for the option you did not choose. Then record the household's response.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Can several attractive benefits compensate for blocking the only agreed access route? **Answer:** not without resolving that access requirement with the people affected. **Reason:** a numerical total or attractive illustration cannot erase a necessary condition.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The choice follows the brief and evidence, acknowledges a trade-off and specifies a reason to reconsider. A principle's name alone is not a justification.

sections.title: App companion for D3
sections.text: Design and evidence guides. Keep versions of alternative concepts; do not overwrite the existing base or silently change measured features when comparing layouts.

units.title: Develop and check the plan
units.output: A checked layout, connected systems and a readable plan set.
units.context: Status: three English reserve drafts. The busy-yard case has no measured source pack yet. A worked scaled layout and its visual checks must be supplied before these lessons can be released as a complete demonstrated sequence. The text below does not certify that missing deliverable.

lessons.title: Move from a concept to a measured layout

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: A proposed bed fits on a sketch. What must be known before saying it fits on the ground?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
A concept explains an arrangement. A developed layout must also show whether its parts fit the available space. Return to the base-map measurements. Check the boundaries relevant to the work, the existing features, access and the distances needed to place the proposal. Keep the measurement method and units with the record.

Use a consistent scale for the plan. Check a known distance against that scale rather than trusting how large the picture looks on a screen. Resizing an image can change its printed scale. A dimension label and the drawn geometry should agree; if they disagree, find the source of the error before using either.

Allow for working access and the needs of the selected system. Do not borrow a universal spacing from a decorative drawing. Use the approved technical source for the actual crop, structure or system, including growth and maintenance needs. If the required dimension is unknown, mark that part incomplete.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: MAP-A is not to scale. The busy-yard learner cannot yet prove that a new bed fits beside the route. They list the measurements needed and preserve the existing path. The correct next step is to obtain a suitable measured base, not shrink the path until the picture looks finished.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: On a measured practice site supplied by the facilitator, reconcile the written dimensions, units and scaled drawing. Point to the information that establishes fit. On your own design, mark any proposal still awaiting measurement or technical dimensions. Do not conduct unsafe or specialist surveying as an unsupervised course task.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Does zooming in on the app make an estimated distance more accurate? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** zoom changes the view, not the measurement source.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner uses consistent units, checks fit against evidence and refuses to claim missing dimensions. This task cannot be passed from the unmeasured busy-yard sketch alone.

lessons.title: Check the connections before approving work

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: Every planned feature fits within the boundary. Is the whole plan ready to implement?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
Fitting the objects is only one check. Follow the people, water, materials and maintenance journeys between them. Check that a route remains usable when people carry tools or produce. Ask whether a mature planting or a stored material could obstruct access that is clear in today's drawing.

Look beyond the selected area. A water change can affect places downstream; a fence can affect shared access. Record the people and resources affected. The design folder should identify relevant permissions and technical advice, not assume them from a boundary line or software tool.

Ask how the system behaves when something goes wrong. If supply is interrupted, who responds? If a component blocks or overflows, where could the problem go? Technical designs need appropriate assessment; do not invent a safe outlet or drainage capacity. When evidence is incomplete, hold the affected work and explain the dependency.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The busy-yard proposal keeps the route visible, but the learner still checks it with its users. A new tank remains only an idea: water demand, supply, siting, support, cost and overflow are not established. The design can progress in other areas while that proposal remains unresolved.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Walk through the proposed daily routine using the map. Mark a possible conflict, the evidence needed to resolve it and who should help. Check both normal use and a relevant disruption. Refer to the technical modules rather than supplying a guessed dimension or capacity.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Does the presence of a Water or Earthworks tool mean any placement it accepts is suitable? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** drawing software does not replace site-specific assessment or permission.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner checks relationships and consequences, identifies an unresolved dependency and keeps the corresponding work conditional.

lessons.title: Make a plan another person can read

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: A map has beautiful plants but no distinction between existing and proposed features. What might the person doing the work misunderstand?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
A plan communicates decisions. Give it a clear title, revision and purpose. Show orientation, scale status, units, legend and sources. Distinguish existing features from proposed changes and unresolved information using labels or patterns as well as colour. Keep labels near the correct features without covering essential details.

Separate information when a single sheet becomes crowded. A base map, analysis overlay, proposal and phase sheet can tell different parts of the same story. Keep feature names and references consistent between them. The cost record and care plan should refer to the same items shown on the map.

Inspect the actual export at the size it will be used. Can someone read it on a phone or printed sheet? Are labels clipped? Does the legend describe things that are really present? Does decorative artwork hide a path or imply features that were never recorded? Correct the output and check again.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: MAP-A keeps its “not to scale” status in every export. A proposal view must not lose that limitation merely because it receives a polished background. The learner uses separate labels for the retained patch and any future idea.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Give the plan to a partner without explaining it first. Ask them to identify what exists, what is proposed, where access runs and which work is still on hold. Record the confusion, revise the sheet and repeat the reading task.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Is an AI illustration evidence that the saved plan contains the same geometry? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** the illustration and measured plan have different evidential roles; inspect the actual plan and its sources.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: Another reader can correctly interpret the plan, and the learner has checked a real export. An export button being clicked is not sufficient.

sections.title: App companion for D4
sections.text: Mapping, design and exports guides. Compare the saved dimensions and exported view; preserve the original geometry when improving presentation. No paid render is required.

units.title: Plan the work and ongoing care
units.output: A feasible sequence, cost record and agreed care plan.
units.context: Status: three English reserve drafts. These connect design reasoning to the separate finance course. No local price, work rate, construction specification or completion date is supplied as a recommendation.

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: Plants have been bought, but the proposed area has no agreed care or reliable water arrangement. Which dependency was missed?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
A phase is a manageable part of the work. Its place in the sequence depends on what must be ready first. Start with the design decision, then list its prerequisites: permission, measurements, advice, suitable materials, resources, access and the people who will care for it.

Distinguish investigating from implementing. Obtaining a quotation does not commit you to buying. Marking a proposed area for discussion does not authorise digging. A design may have useful information-gathering steps even while construction is on hold.

Choose a first phase that answers the household brief and fits the resources actually agreed. Keep access and existing useful systems working during the change. Describe what would make the phase ready to begin, what would stop it and how you will check its result. Do not begin every component simply because all of them appear in the final vision.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The busy-yard first phase begins with checking care capacity, access and the existing patch's conditions. Buying animals is outside scope. A new drainage intervention stays on hold. Improving the design record is real progress even before a physical change is justified.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Make an ordered list with an action, prerequisites, responsible person, readiness evidence and next review point. Ask a partner to find something that has been placed before its prerequisite. Correct the sequence and explain why.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Is a proposed planting phase ready because the seedlings are available? **Answer:** not from that fact alone. **Reason:** the destination, suitable conditions, resources and continuing care also need to be ready.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner identifies dependencies and a feasible first phase, rather than a calendar of unsupported promises.

lessons.title: Connect the drawing to quantities and money

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: The drawing includes a tank and fence, but the budget has only a plant purchase. Does the budget describe the plan?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
Give proposed items consistent references across the plan and cost record. Derive quantities from a checked design or record their source. Keep unknown quantities unknown. Ask for suitable quotations when a purchase is being considered; do not turn a remembered price into a current supplier offer.

Include the work and supporting materials needed for the proposal, not only its most visible object. Separate one-time purchases from ongoing care costs. Record household contributions honestly. A donated material can still require transport, preparation or maintenance; a volunteer's time still needs agreement.

The date money is needed matters. A future sale does not pay today's bill unless funding is actually available. Use the finance lessons to keep budgets, dated cash forecasts, actual payments and amounts owed distinct. Do not count a hoped-for harvest as confirmed cash or a device-generated plan as proof of profitability.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: RESOURCES-A contains no prices, quantities or committed labour. The busy-yard learner creates an unknown-cost register with evidence needed for each proposed change. They cannot claim that concept A is affordable merely because it retains the old patch.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Choose a proposed item and trace it from the plan to its quantity source, quotation or unknown, payment timing and care cost. State what the current record includes and excludes. Compare the first phase with available resources before committing to it.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Should an unpriced item be entered as zero to make the total work? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** zero states a known value; missing information requires a separate unknown and a follow-up action.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The plan and budget describe the same scope; the learner preserves exclusions, unknowns and cash timing. No purchase is needed to demonstrate the method.

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: A project has an installation team but no agreed person to look after it afterwards. What is incomplete?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
A design continues after installation. Ask what must be checked, maintained, cleaned, repaired, harvested or recorded. Use the relevant technical lesson and local advice to establish the actual task. Do not assign a generic weekly schedule to living systems with different care needs.

Agree who will do each task and what they need. Ask about normal commitments and absences. A task is not allocated just because a name appears beside it; the person must understand and accept the responsibility. Plan how they will ask for help and what can be reduced if the workload is too much.

Identify relevant disruptions. Water interruptions, damaged access, a missing carer or unavailable materials may change what is feasible. Define a response that preserves welfare and safety. Where the answer depends on specialist advice, record that dependency instead of inventing an emergency procedure.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The person carrying water in the busy-yard case helps review the care plan. The design does not assume they can take on extra work. If care capacity remains unknown, expansion stays conditional while the household tests its existing routine.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Make a care sheet with task, reason, responsible person, required resources, evidence-based timing or trigger, backup arrangement and record. Discuss a disruption with the household or practice partner and revise the proposal if its care cannot be supported.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Can an installation photograph show that ongoing care has been arranged? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** it records appearance at a moment; care requires responsibilities, resources and follow-up evidence.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner distinguishes installation from maintenance, records agreement and shows how care capacity affects scope.

sections.title: App companion for D5
sections.text: Finance, expenses and crop-planning guides. Use classroom/sample records for practice and keep unknowns visible where an app field cannot represent them safely. The guide is not a substitute for the design's care plan.

units.title: Explain, test and improve
units.output: An explained design, monitoring approach and justified revision.
units.context: Status: three English reserve drafts. The reserve integrated capstone rubric is the assessment starting point. These lessons do not award course credit or claim professional accreditation.

lessons.title: Present the reasoning behind the plan

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: A learner names every feature on a map. Have they explained why the design meets the household's needs?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
Begin a design presentation with the brief. Show the existing situation and the evidence that mattered most. Then explain the chosen arrangement, an alternative you considered, the important trade-off and the first feasible phase. Keep unknowns visible; explaining a limitation is better than hiding it behind a confident picture.

Choose a format the learner can use: drawings, a printed map, spoken explanation, supported notes or the app. Assess the reasoning and relevant evidence rather than fluency with a device. Ask for consent before recording or sharing a person's presentation.

Invite specific feedback. A reviewer can name a supported strength, a missing assumption and a question that might change the plan. Listen before defending the drawing. Record whether the question exposes missing evidence, a misunderstanding in the presentation or a genuine conflict in the design.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The busy-yard learner explains why access and care shaped the provisional choice. They show that water and measurements are still unresolved. A claim that the plan is ready to construct would not follow from that evidence, however attractive the presentation.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Present your folder to a partner. Ask them to trace a decision from brief to evidence to proposal. Record their question and your answer or next check. Use the capstone criteria to identify anything not yet demonstrated.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Does a confident presentation resolve an unknown water supply? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** speaking clearly can communicate evidence; it cannot create missing evidence.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner explains the choice and its limits, responds to a substantive question and identifies a justified next action.

lessons.title: Observe whether the design is helping

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: A growing area looks green after rain. Does that prove the design has met the household's food and workload goals?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
Decide what to observe from the goals in the brief. If access was a priority, ask its users whether the route works and observe it under relevant conditions. If care was a concern, record the tasks and difficulties. A harvest record can inform food production, but it does not alone prove improved household nutrition or income.

Keep a starting record so later observations have context. Record what was actually implemented, when, and any changes from the plan. Note the conditions and other events that may influence the result. Do not attribute every improvement or setback to the design without considering other explanations.

A short course cannot show a whole seasonal outcome. Agree a follow-up appropriate to the decision and the situation, with actual dates set during delivery. If no implementation has occurred, assess the plan and reasoning as such. Do not substitute a generated picture or imagined harvest for observed results.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: The busy-yard brief suggests following access usability and care demands. There is no claimed later harvest or success story in the supplied case. The learner prepares an observation sheet and explains what would count as useful evidence; they cannot fill it with invented results.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Link each priority to an observation, a source or method, the person responsible and an agreed review point. State what the observation can and cannot demonstrate. Use practice data only if clearly labelled as supplied classroom data.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Does a photograph establish that income increased? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** that claim needs appropriate financial evidence and context, not appearance alone.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The monitoring plan matches the brief and distinguishes planned, reported and observed results. No outcome is claimed before evidence exists.

lessons.title: Revise and hand over a usable plan

sections.title: Question to show
sections.text: New evidence changes a placement decision. Should the old plan disappear without a record of what changed?

sections.title: Teaching text
sections.text:
Revision is part of design. Keep the previous version, identify the new evidence and explain which decision changes. Check the connected records as well as the drawing. Moving a feature may change access, quantities, costs, water needs or care. A revised map with an old budget can tell a misleading story.

Agree the revised scope with the people affected. Separate work that can proceed from work still needing evidence or advice. Give the person taking over the current plan, source notes, implementation sequence, care responsibilities and unresolved actions. Make the information available in a format they can use without your presence.

Use feedback to plan another attempt where a skill is not yet demonstrated. Finishing the course pages, attending sessions or exporting a map are different from demonstrating the whole design process. Record the actual evidence behind the assessment, and do not turn a course completion label into unsupported specialist authority.

sections.title: Worked example
sections.text: If later busy-yard evidence shows that the preferred option cannot preserve access, the learner returns to the alternatives. That is a conditional teaching example, not a reported event. The revision would update the plan, decision record, cost scope and care discussion together.

sections.title: Learner task
sections.text: Make a revision record with the question, new evidence, affected decision, change and connected records updated. Ask a partner to use the handover pack to explain the next action and what remains on hold. If they cannot, improve the pack and try again.

sections.title: Check
sections.text: Is changing only the picture enough when the proposal's material quantities change? **Answer:** no. **Reason:** linked quantities, cost assumptions and implementation information must also be checked.

sections.title: Evidence for feedback
sections.text: The learner explains a justified revision, preserves its reason and produces a usable handover. The facilitator records demonstrated, needs another attempt or not yet observed with evidence.

sections.title: App companion for D6
sections.text: Evidence, design and exports guides. Inspect the saved and exported revision, retain the previous record and share only with the household's agreement. A paper/oral handover remains valid.

case.text:
# Worked household case — the busy yard

All people, observations and events below are invented for classroom discussion. They are not a report of a real household or evidence of an intervention's success. There are no supplied dimensions, rainfall totals, water quantities, costs, yields or plant identities. Do not infer them from a future illustration.

## Stable starting facts

**BRIEF-A — household discussion.** The household wants vegetables for meals, a route that stays usable between the home and gate, and care work that can fit existing commitments. It does not want animals added in this first phase. The person who usually carries water asks to be included in siting decisions. Another household member needs a route without obstructions. The household agrees to explore options in its existing yard, but that agreement is not a verified boundary survey or permission for work beyond the yard.

**WALK-A — initial visit.** A used route crosses the yard between the home and gate. The existing growing patch lies beside that route. A water point is beside the home. Containers are carried from it to the patch. The eastern part of the yard is shaded during this visit. These observations say nothing yet about the full seasonal shade pattern, water pressure, available volume, water quality or production potential.

**TALK-A — reported history.** A resident says water has crossed the eastern part during heavy rain. No rain is falling on the first visit. Record the resident's experience as reported information, with consent; do not replace it with an invented slope arrow or present it as a measured flood level.

**MAP-A — first sketch.** It locates the home, gate, used route, water point, existing patch and the area mentioned in TALK-A relative to each other. It is labelled “not to scale; boundary, north and dimensions need checking”. No compass direction is derived from an unverified photograph. The supplied statement that part of the yard is eastern is a case description, not a direction the learner has measured.

**RESOURCES-A — current limits.** Available care time, reliable water supply, soil conditions, material quantities and costs are not yet recorded. No other person's labour or money is promised. No neighbour's land, water route or access is available merely because it appears on a picture.

## Worked decisions through the first two stages

### D1 — what is the task?

The brief prioritises food, usable access and manageable care. Adding a pond or animals is not a stated need. The facilitator asks the people doing the work what they can maintain and what must remain clear. The learner records missing resource information instead of assigning an imaginary budget.

On the first map the growing patch is an existing feature. An idea for a new patch belongs on a proposal overlay. The learner does not erase the used route because it interrupts the picture. The family report about rain is kept beside its source; it is not changed into an observed event.

### D2 — what do the facts mean?

The daily watering journey makes convenient access worth investigating. It does not prove that the closest possible location is suitable. The shade snapshot needs further seasonal evidence, and the reported water route needs examination before considering an intervention.

The learner writes: “Can we improve care of the existing patch while keeping the route usable?” This is a design question. “Build a swale through the eastern yard” would jump past the missing terrain, water, suitability and permission evidence.

For the next safe visit, the learner asks the household to show how people move through the space. They arrange further shade observations and ask who can help assess the reported water problem. They do not enter dangerous runoff to obtain a photograph. They keep all three options open: improve the existing patch, consider another suitable location, or defer expansion until resources are known.

## D3 — concept comparison, still conditional

Concept A investigates improving care of the existing patch. Concept B investigates a different location while retaining the access route. Both must meet BRIEF-A. A has not been shown to cost less; B has not been shown to produce more. Both still need the resource and site checks recorded in D1–D2. The provisional preference for investigating A is based on manageable care and existing access, not an invented performance advantage. Do not add new dimensions or resource quantities silently. When a later source card supplies information, identify what changed, why it is credible within the case and which earlier decision it affects.

A completed worked example must eventually show a scaled source pack, concept comparison, developed layout, dependencies and care, a cost/unknown record and a revision after feedback. This file currently supplies the brief, analysis and conditional concept comparison; it is not that completed example. D4–D6 lesson text is drafted, but the measured demonstration, actual plan set and supplied later-evidence/revision exercise remain unfinished.
